## **About **

I'm a full-stack developer and open source contributor. My core stack is PHP with Laravel, and I'm equally at home with Node.js and Vue.js on the front end, plus Rust where performance matters.

Right now I'm building [Countdown Builder](https://countdownbuilder.com) and [OG Dynamic](https://ogdynamic.com).

---

- **Page:** Real client IPs through the stream hop, with PROXY protocol
- **Source:** https://mehedi.im/blog/nginx-proxy-protocol
- **Description:** The stream hop forwards raw TCP, so nothing downstream ever saw the visitor. PROXY protocol fixes that — here's the setup and the traps that come with it.

![PROXY protocol across the stream hop](https://mehedi.im/images/blog/banner-proxy-protocol-light.png)

At the end of [the unix socket swap](https://mehedi.im/blog/nginx-stream-unix-sockets) I left a loose end: my analytics for customer domains had quietly turned into one visitor. The `stream` block forwards raw TCP, so nothing downstream knows who connected — and once the hops moved to sockets, downstream doesn't even get an address. The peer on a unix socket is just "unix".

This post is the fix: PROXY protocol across the same sockets, and what it took to get Caddy and Nginx to speak it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    V["Visitor<br>203.0.113.50"] -->|HTTPS :443| N["Nginx stream (L4)"]
    N -->|"unix socket + PROXY line"| H["Nginx http · ssl"]
    N -->|"SNI: custom domain · socket + PROXY line"| C["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
    H -->|"$remote_addr = visitor"| App["App"]
    C -->|"{remote_host} = visitor"| App
```

## Why the address disappears

The stream server terminates nothing. It peeks at the SNI, picks a backend, and copies bytes from one file descriptor to another. It never parses HTTP, so it can't add headers — there's no HTTP to attach anything to. And it can't decrypt to find out either; that's the whole point of the hop.

So Caddy's idea of the remote address is Nginx's connection, and the app's idea is Caddy. Rate limiting, abuse blocking, logs, analytics: they all see one client. The socket swap made it starker — over loopback TCP at least everyone agreed on `127.0.0.1`; over a unix socket the peer address is a path that tells you nothing.

## What PROXY protocol is

A short plaintext line that the stream block prepends to the connection, before the TLS handshake:

```text
PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.50 10.0.0.5 51234 443
```

The backend reads the line, strips it, and treats `203.0.113.50` as the connection's remote address. TLS then proceeds untouched — the ClientHello is byte-for-byte what the visitor sent.

One thing to be clear about: the header is a claim, not proof. Whoever can connect to a PROXY-protocol listener can send `PROXY TCP4 1.2.3.4 ...` and impersonate any IP, which quietly defeats rate limits and bans. This is where the `0750` socket directory from the last post stops being a nice-to-have: only Caddy and the Nginx group can reach these listeners at all. On loopback TCP, every process on the box could.

## Sending it from stream

```nginx
server {
    listen 443;
    ssl_preread on;
    proxy_pass $https_backend;
    proxy_protocol on;
}
```

The trap is that this is all-or-nothing. `proxy_protocol on` prefixes every connection this server forwards, including the ones headed for the main app. **Every backend in the map must accept PROXY protocol, or none of them can.**

## The Caddy side

Caddy speaks PROXY protocol through a listener wrapper:

```caddy
{
    http_port 8082

    on_demand_tls {
        ask http://127.0.0.1:8000/internal/domain-check
    }

    servers unix//run/app-sockets/caddy-tls.sock|0666 {
        protocols h1 h2
        listener_wrappers {
            proxy_protocol
            tls
        }
    }
}
```

Three details, and I hit all three:

- **The directive is listener_wrappers.** I typed `listen_wrappers` first and got `unrecognized servers option`.
- **Order matters.** `proxy_protocol` must come before `tls`, because the PROXY line arrives before the ClientHello. Reverse them and Caddy tries to parse `PROXY TCP4...` as a TLS handshake.
- **Scope it to the socket.** A bare `servers { }` applies to every listener, including plain HTTP on 8082 — and a `tls` wrapper on an ACME port breaks HTTP-01 challenges and the redirect. The address after `servers` has to match the listener Caddy actually creates, and a mismatch fails silently: `caddy validate` still passes. Check it with adapt:

```bash
sudo caddy adapt --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile --pretty | grep -n -B3 -A10 listener_wrappers
```

You want `proxy_protocol` then `tls` inside a server whose `listen` is the socket path. If the block is missing, copy the exact `"listen"` string from the adapt output into the `servers` line.

(`protocols h1 h2` is there because the socket carries TCP only — there's no UDP on it for HTTP/3.)

## The main app has to accept it too

The other backend in the map is Nginx's own `http` server. Its `listen` line gains a parameter, plus two directives to actually use the header:

```nginx
listen unix:/run/app-sockets/nginx-app.sock ssl proxy_protocol;

set_real_ip_from unix:;
real_ip_header   proxy_protocol;
```

`proxy_protocol` on the `listen` line makes Nginx *parse* the line. `set_real_ip_from` together with `real_ip_header proxy_protocol` makes it *use* the line to set `$remote_addr`. You need both — parse alone just strips the header and leaves you back at "no useful address". For a unix socket peer, the trusted source is `unix:`.

Because one side now sends the header and the other side *requires* it, there's no rolling this out one backend at a time. Switch both sides together:

```bash
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl restart caddy && sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

## What this buys downstream

With the wrapper in place, `{remote_host}` in Caddy resolves to the visitor, so anything it proxies can pass the address on:

```caddy
reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
    header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
}
```

And in the Nginx `http` block, `$remote_addr` is the visitor again — which rate limiting and logs pick up with no further config.

## How I verified it

A page that loads proves nothing. I checked each path separately, from a machine other than the server:

```bash
curl -s ifconfig.me                                # your public IP
curl -s https://timer.customer.com/check-ip        # customer-domain path
curl -s https://app.example.com/check-ip           # main-app path
```

Both `/check-ip` endpoints should print your public IP. (`ifconfig.me` may answer over IPv6 while your other path returns IPv4; force a family with `-4` or `-6` if they disagree.)

## What I'd tell past me

1. Treat `proxy_protocol` as a change to the whole proxy chain, not one backend. Every backend in the map accepts it, or none can — and both sides switch together.
2. After editing `servers <address>` in Caddy, run `caddy adapt` and confirm the wrapper attached. `validate` passing doesn't prove it.
3. Check real client IPs in the logs on day one, not after a week of bad analytics.

---

- **Page:** I moved Nginx's internal hops to Unix sockets
- **Source:** https://mehedi.im/blog/nginx-stream-unix-sockets
- **Description:** My stream block was opening TCP connections to Nginx itself and to Caddy, even though neither hop ever leaves the machine. Here's the move to Unix sockets, the network overhead it drops, and what I left alone.

![Unix sockets for the internal Nginx hops](https://mehedi.im/images/blog/banner-unix-sockets-light.png)

In [Multi-Tenant Custom Domains](https://mehedi.im/blog/multi-tenant-custom-domains) I finished with an Nginx `stream` block on 443 that reads the SNI and forwards the connection. Known domains went to `127.0.0.1:8081`, where a normal `http` server handled TLS. Everything else went to Caddy on `127.0.0.1:8443`.

It worked fine. It also bugged me, because both of those hops are just processes on the same machine talking to each other over TCP. One of them is Nginx connecting to itself.

So I swapped both for Unix sockets. The main reason is simple: these hops never leave the machine, so they shouldn't be paying for the network stack at all.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Client] -->|HTTPS :443| N["Nginx stream (L4)"]
    N -->|unix socket| H["Nginx http · ssl"]
    N -->|"SNI: custom domain · unix socket"| C["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
    H -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App["App"]
    C -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App
```

## Why bother

Both hops are processes on the same machine talking to each other. Over TCP that means a full handshake, loopback addressing, ephemeral ports, and `TIME_WAIT` cleanup on every connection — the kernel running its whole networking routine for a conversation that never leaves the box.

A Unix socket skips all of it. The kernel moves bytes directly between the two processes, and there's no network stack in the path. You also drop two arbitrary port numbers that someone, probably you in six months, will have to wonder about.

The socket being a file has a side effect I like too: to connect, you need permission on the socket and on the directory it lives in. Everything here is on one machine that I control, so that's not what drove the change — but it costs nothing.

## One directory for all of them

I put both sockets in the same directory, so there's one place to check and one permission rule to reason about:

```bash
echo 'd /run/app-sockets 0750 caddy www-data -' | sudo tee /etc/tmpfiles.d/app-sockets.conf
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create
```

The directory belongs to `caddy`, with group `www-data` and mode `0750`. Check which user your Nginx workers run as (`grep '^user' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf`) and use that as the group if it isn't `www-data`.

You might wonder how Nginx creates a socket in a directory its workers can't write to. It doesn't need the workers for that. The master process runs as root and creates the listening sockets at startup. The workers, running as `www-data`, only have to walk into the directory and connect, and the group's read and execute bits cover that.

I put it under `/run` rather than `/tmp` because `/run` is tmpfs. The directory and any stale sockets disappear on reboot, and the tmpfiles rule recreates the directory at boot.

## The Nginx side

This is the stream map from the last post, with the targets swapped for socket paths:

```nginx
stream {
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $https_backend {
        app.example.com  unix:/run/app-sockets/nginx-app.sock;
        example.com      unix:/run/app-sockets/nginx-app.sock;
        default          unix:/run/app-sockets/caddy-tls.sock;
    }

    server {
        listen 443;
        ssl_preread on;
        proxy_pass $https_backend;
    }
}
```

The `unix:` prefix is required in the map values. The `http` server for the main app used to say `listen 127.0.0.1:8081 ssl;`, and now it says:

```nginx
listen unix:/run/app-sockets/nginx-app.sock ssl;
```

Nothing else in that block changes. The TLS handshake passes through the socket exactly as it did over TCP, the SNI is still in the ClientHello, and `server_name` and certificate selection keep working. The map value and the `listen` line have to match exactly. Copy one from the other instead of retyping.

## The Caddy side

Caddy can bind a site to a socket with `bind`. I also dropped `https_port 8443`, since there's no port anymore:

```caddy
{
    http_port 8082

    on_demand_tls {
        ask http://127.0.0.1:8000/internal/domain-check
    }
}

https:// {
    bind unix//run/app-sockets/caddy-tls.sock|0666

    tls {
        on_demand
    }

    # ...the rest of your handlers, unchanged
}
```

The `|0666` is the socket's file mode. I set it explicitly so the Nginx worker is certain to be able to connect. It looks wide open, but remember the directory is `0750`, so only `caddy` and the Nginx group can get to the file at all.

`http_port 8082` stays a normal TCP port. Port 80 doesn't go through the `stream` block. It's handled by a regular `http` block that proxies to Caddy for ACME HTTP-01 challenges and the redirect, so that path isn't part of this change.

## Switching over

Do Caddy first, so the socket exists before Nginx starts sending to it:

```bash
sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl restart caddy && sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

I'd do this one hop at a time the first time. Move the Nginx app hop, check the main site, then do Caddy. If something breaks, you know which half caused it.

## What I left on TCP

The app itself still listens on plain HTTP over loopback. `proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:...` in Nginx and `reverse_proxy` in Caddy are exactly as they were.

Sockets make sense when you control both ends and the connection never needs to leave the machine. For the Nginx-to-Nginx and Nginx-to-Caddy hops, that's true. The app is a separate process with its own lifecycle, and it's also what `curl` and health checks talk to. Keeping that boring is worth more to me than a slightly shorter path.

## Bookkeeping, not bandwidth

To be clear about what you're dropping: it's bookkeeping, not bandwidth. You skip the TCP handshake and the kernel's per-connection networking work on these hops. There are no ports involved, so there's no `TIME_WAIT` pile on the closing side after a burst of connections. That's exactly the overhead I wanted gone on hops that don't need a network — I'm just not going to claim you'll feel it in a benchmark. If you want to see the `TIME_WAIT` difference yourself, count them before and after:

```bash
ss -tan state time-wait | grep -E ':8081|:8443' | wc -l
```

After the switch that should be zero, because those ports don't exist.

## When it breaks

The error log is clear about it. These are the ones I'd expect:

- **connect() to unix:/run/app-sockets/... failed (2: No such file or directory).** Nothing is listening on that path. Usually the map value and the `listen` line don't match, or Caddy hasn't been restarted yet.
- **(13: Permission denied).** The worker can't reach the socket. Check `ls -ld /run/app-sockets` (owner `caddy`, group matching your Nginx user, mode `0750`) and which user the workers run as.

## How I checked it

```bash
ls -l /run/app-sockets/
ss -xlp | grep app-sockets      # both sockets listening
ss -tlnp | grep -E ':8081|:8443'  # should print nothing
curl -sI https://app.example.com/
curl --resolve timer.customer.com:443:YOUR_SERVER_IP -sI https://timer.customer.com/
```

The first three confirm the sockets exist and the old ports are gone. The two `curl` calls run the real path end to end, and one is for a customer domain, so you know Caddy is serving through its socket. I also checked that certificate issuance still worked for a domain that had never hit the server.

You can also test the app's socket directly, skipping the `stream` layer. This needs `sudo`, because your shell user isn't in the directory's group:

```bash
sudo curl --unix-socket /run/app-sockets/nginx-app.sock -sI https://app.example.com/
```

## One thing it broke

Before the switch, the `http` block saw `127.0.0.1` as the client. Now over a socket it sees no useful address at all. And Caddy still only sees Nginx, not the real visitor. The `stream` hop forwards raw TCP, so nothing downstream knows who connected. My analytics for customer domains quietly turned into one visitor.

Fixing that takes PROXY protocol, and it has a couple of traps. That's the next post.

---

**Read next:** [Real client IPs through the stream hop, with PROXY protocol](https://mehedi.im/blog/nginx-proxy-protocol) — the fix for that one-visitor analytics, and the traps along the way.

---

- **Page:** Multi-Tenant Custom Domains, without paying for Cloudflare for SaaS
- **Source:** https://mehedi.im/blog/multi-tenant-custom-domains
- **Description:** How Countdown Builder serves customer domains with their own TLS certs — Nginx stream SNI routing and Caddy on-demand TLS on a single server.

![Multi-Tenant Custom Domains](https://mehedi.im/images/blog/banner-custom-domains-light.png)

I run [Countdown Builder](https://countdownbuilder.com), a SaaS that serves live countdown timer images for emails. Customers wanted `timer.theirbrand.com` instead of our domain, which meant issuing and renewing TLS certs for domains I don't know in advance.

Cloudflare for SaaS solves this, but I wanted to keep it on the single server I already run. So I built it with Nginx and Caddy. This is the loop I went through: what I tried, what broke, and what the final setup looks like.

## The final architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Client] -->|HTTPS :443| N["Nginx stream (L4)"]
    N -->|"SNI: known SaaS domain"| App["Nginx app"]
    N -->|"SNI: custom domain"| Caddy["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
```

- **Nginx stream (Layer 4)** listens on 443. It never decrypts anything. It reads the SNI from the TLS handshake and routes the raw connection.
- **Caddy (Layer 7)** handles unknown customer domains. It terminates TLS, gets Let's Encrypt certificates on the fly, and proxies to the backend.

## Attempt 1: Plain Nginx

**Try:** one `server` block with `server_name _` and a wildcard cert.
**Result:** a wildcard cert only covers *my* domain. Customer domains throw certificate warnings, and Gmail's image proxy refuses to fetch the timer.
**Learned:** Nginx needs a cert *before* it knows which site you wanted. Dynamic domains need something that can get certs at handshake time.

## Attempt 2: Caddy on-demand TLS, alone

**Try:** Caddy on 443 with `on_demand` and an `ask` endpoint.
**Result:** it works, but now Caddy fronts my main app too, and I didn't want to migrate a working Nginx setup.
**Learned:** I wanted the main app untouched, with only unknown domains going to Caddy.

## Attempt 3: Nginx `stream` as an SNI router

Nginx's `stream` module can read the SNI from the TLS ClientHello without decrypting anything:

```nginx
stream {
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $https_backend {
        app.example.com  127.0.0.1:8081;   # main app (Nginx http block)
        example.com      127.0.0.1:8081;
        default          127.0.0.1:8443;   # everything else -> Caddy
    }

    server {
        listen 443;
        ssl_preread on;
        proxy_pass $https_backend;
    }
}
```

**Result:** HTTPS worked. Known domains hit the app, unknown ones hit Caddy and got certs on demand. I thought I was done.

## Port 80 routing doesn't work in `stream`

My first draft routed port 80 with `$http_host` inside a `stream` map. That variable doesn't exist there, because stream is Layer 4 and never parses HTTP. You get a config error or an empty variable, depending on version.

**Fix:** keep port 80 in a normal `http` block, where Host-based routing works:

```nginx
http {
    server {
        listen 80 default_server;
        server_name app.example.com example.com;
        location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:5000; }
    }

    server {
        listen 80;
        server_name _;
        location / {
            proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8082;   # Caddy HTTP (ACME + redirect)
            proxy_set_header Host $host;
        }
    }
}
```

## The gatekeeper endpoint

Without an `ask` endpoint, anyone can point a domain at your IP and make Caddy burn through your Let's Encrypt rate limits. Caddy calls your backend before issuing:

```http
GET /internal/domain-check?domain=clientdomain.com
```

- **200 OK:** your database recognizes the domain. Caddy gets the cert, caches it, and serves the request.
- **Anything else:** Caddy aborts the handshake.

Keep it to one indexed DB lookup, since it sits on the handshake path.

## Gotcha: ACME challenges and scanner noise

HTTP-01 needs port 80 to reach Caddy for the customer domain, which the `http` block from Bug 1 handles. If issuance fails, check first that the customer's DNS actually points at your server.

You may also see `tls-alpn challenge ... no information found to solve challenge for identifier:` in Caddy's logs every few days. Look at the `server_name` field: when it's empty, something connected with the ACME ALPN protocol but sent no hostname. Real validations carry the domain, so this is almost certainly a scanner, and Caddy is correctly refusing it.

## How I verified it

A page that loads proves nothing. I checked each path separately, from a machine other than the server:

```bash
curl -sI https://timer.customer.com/        # customer-domain path
curl -sI https://app.example.com/           # main-app path
```

Both should answer over HTTPS with no certificate warnings. To inspect the certificate Caddy actually issued:

```bash
echo | openssl s_client -connect timer.customer.com:443 -servername timer.customer.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
```

That should show Let's Encrypt as the issuer, with dates that make sense.

Last, issue a certificate for a domain that has never touched the server and read Caddy's log:

```bash
sudo journalctl -u caddy --since "5 min ago" --no-pager | grep -iE 'obtaining|obtained|error'
```

You want `obtaining new certificate` followed by `certificate obtained successfully`. (If journalctl prints "No entries" without `sudo`, that's a permissions issue, not an empty log.)

## What I'd tell past me

1. Prototype with Let's Encrypt **staging** to avoid rate limits while debugging.
2. Test with `curl --resolve` before touching real DNS.
3. Add a per-domain issuance cap in your `ask` endpoint.

---

**Read next:** [I moved Nginx's internal hops to Unix sockets](https://mehedi.im/blog/nginx-stream-unix-sockets) — the stream block now hands off to the HTTP block and to Caddy over sockets, while the app keeps its plain HTTP listener.
